turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, they sent me here... my lieutenant sent me here. I was at the station, you know, waiting on a call, and I was moving the airway bags. I had to arrange them in a specific pattern, the one I just knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Seven-four-two, eight-one-nine... numbers are funny like that, you know? My grandfather used to play the numbers game back in Chicago, always said you had to listen to the rhythm of the city to get the right ones. He had this old radio that picked up police bands. Anyway, I wouldn't step away from the bags when my lieutenant told me to stop. I couldn't. It felt like... like the whole ambulance bay would go bad, just rot or something, if I broke the sequence. Kind of like how you have to check the oil in the rig before every shift, except if you don't do this, everything just stops working.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient displays tangential speech, drifting from dispatch numbers to an unrelated story about their grandfather in Chicago.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes inappropriate, repetitive behavior at work and negativism by refusing to step away when ordered by their lieutenant.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient describes compulsive ordering, arranging, and repeating rituals performed to prevent an unrealistic feared outcome (the ambulance bay going bad).

turns.doctor_question: When you were repeating those numbers and arranging the bags, did it feel like something you wanted to do, or did it feel like a forced, distressing urge that you were trying to resist?
turns.patient_response: I don't really know if I wanted to... it wasn't really about wanting. I'm not sure what you mean by resisting it, either. It just was. You know those airway bags, the blue pediatric ones? They're made of this really heavy canvas material. Canvas is weird, it holds onto smells forever. Mostly copper and bleach. We use so much bleach on the rig to wipe down the gurney after a bad call. My partner, Dave, he absolutely hates the smell of bleach. He says it reminds him of his ex-wife's hair salon. She used to do highlights all day. Frosting, I think they called it back in the 90s. My sister got her hair frosted once before prom. She looked like a zebra. Did you ever have frosted tips, Doc? A lot of guys did. But yeah, I don't know about the urge thing you're asking about. The numbers just had to go with the canvas handles.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, drifting off-topic from airway bags to bleach, a coworker's ex-wife, and 1990s hair trends.
symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient explicitly denies experiencing a forced, distressing urge or making any attempt to resist the thoughts and behaviors.

turns.doctor_question: When you felt that the ambulance bay would 'go bad' if you didn't finish the sequence, did you believe that there was a literal, physical connection between your actions and the safety of the bay, or did it feel more like a nervous, internal tension that you just had to relieve?
turns.patient_response: A physical connection? I mean, I don't know about tension or whatever. The bay is definitely physical. It's all concrete and steel, you know? Concrete is super porous, actually. If you spill diesel on it, it just drinks it right up and the stain stays there forever. We had this massive diesel spill back in February when it was freezing out. The block heaters on the rigs are always giving out in the cold. Our mechanic, Gary... he's this huge guy, used to work on John Deere tractors down in Peoria before he came up here. He brought in this giant wrench once to fix the bay doors, looked like something out of a cartoon. He always said you need big tools for big problems. Tractors are crazy, they don't go fast but the torque is unbelievable. Have you ever driven a tractor, Doc? It's nothing like driving an ambulance. You definitely don't need sirens out in a cornfield.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the doctor's question about a physical connection to concrete, diesel spills, a mechanic, and finally tractors.

turns.doctor_question: I've noticed that when we talk, your mind seems to jump between many different topics very quickly—do you feel like your thoughts are racing or getting 'mixed up' in a way that makes it hard for you to stay focused on one thing?
turns.patient_response:
Mixed up? I don't really think they're mixed up. They just go how they go, at regular speed. Mixing things up is dangerous though, especially on the job. Like when dispatch mixes up Street and Avenue. One time they sent us to 402 Elm Street instead of Elm Avenue. Avenues always have those big old oak trees lining them around here, you know? Oaks drop so many acorns in the fall. It sounds like hail when they hit the roof of the ambulance. 

My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she spends hours sweeping acorns off her driveway every single morning. She has this really old broom, the kind with real straw bristles. Straw brooms are way better than the plastic ones. Plastic just pushes the dirt around, it doesn't actually sweep anything up. I tried to tell my lieutenant that we should get a straw broom for the station, but he said it's a fire hazard. Fire hazards are everywhere, honestly. Like lint in a dryer. Do you clean your lint trap, Doc? You really have to make sure you do that, or the whole house just goes up in smoke. Everything burns if it gets hot enough.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, jumping rapidly from dispatch errors to oak trees, acorns, brooms, and fire hazards without a logical flow.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient explicitly denies having racing thoughts, stating that their thoughts go at a 'regular speed'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear people talking to you or commenting on your actions when there is actually no one else around?
turns.patient_response: Hearing people? No, I don't really hear anybody if no one's around. I mean, unless you count the portable radio. Those things always have this low-level static going on, like a hiss, even when dispatch isn't saying anything. Snakes hiss, actually. We got called out for a snake bite last summer at the state park. Some guy tried to pick up a copperhead. They blend right into the dead leaves, it's crazy. Fall leaves are the absolute worst to rake up. My dad used to make me bag them in those big brown paper yard bags, and they always rip at the bottom if it rained the night before. Wet paper smells terrible. Kind of like a wet dog. Do you have a dog, Doc? Golden retrievers are supposed to be great, but they shed everywhere. Dog hair always gets stuck in the velcro on our blood pressure cuffs. Velcro was invented by a guy who looked at burrs stuck to his pants after a hike, did you know that? Nature just designs things and we end up copying them.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates severe derailment and loose associations, rapidly shifting topics from radios to snakes, leaves, wet dogs, and the invention of velcro.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing people or voices when no one is around.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about things like the ambulance bay 'going bad' or the numbers needing to be in a specific sequence, do you feel like you have some kind of special or unusual influence over how those events turn out?
turns.patient_response: Special influence? No, I don't... I don't think I have any special powers or anything like that. It's just the sequence. You have to finish the sequence. It's like numbers on a combination lock. You know, those Master Locks we use on the lockers at the station? They're always getting jammed. You have to spin the dial three times to the right to clear it before you even start. My locker is right next to the breakroom, and the smell of old coffee just seeps right into my spare uniform. We use this really cheap coffee brand, comes in a massive red plastic tub. Plastic tubs are good for storing road salt, though. We keep one by the back door of the bay because the ice gets so thick there in January. Ice is super heavy, actually. It brought down a huge power line on 4th Street two years ago. We had to sit there in the rig for four hours waiting for the utility guys. The heater in the back of the ambulance was broken, so we just sat there freezing. Have you ever been that cold, Doc? Where your toes just go completely numb? They say you shouldn't put them in hot water right away because it causes nerve damage. Nerves are weird, they look like little white strings if you ever see them in a bad laceration.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies having any special influence or powers over events, ruling out grandiose delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from combination locks to coffee, road salt, ice, power lines, and nerve damage.

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel that you are the only one who truly understands the importance of these sequences, or that you have been chosen to keep things safe through these actions?
turns.patient_response:
Chosen? No, I wouldn't say I was chosen or anything like that. It's just... I just know the sequences have to be finished. It's just how it is. It's like checking the oxygen tanks at the start of a shift. You have to check the pressure, make sure the O-rings are good. If an O-ring is cracked, it leaks, and you lose all your oxygen. Oxygen is highly flammable, too. We had this one call where a guy was smoking on his home oxygen concentrator. Burned his whole face, his eyebrows were just gone. Hair smells awful when it burns. Like burning tires, almost. 

Did you know tires have steel belts inside the rubber? That's what gives them their shape. When they blow out on the highway, those metal wires shred everything. We hit a gator once—that's what we call blown tire treads on the road—and it completely ripped off the mud flap on the rig. Mud flaps are legally required for commercial vehicles, I think. Commercials on TV are getting so loud lately, don't you think? Like, the show is quiet, and then the commercial blasts your eardrums out. I usually just mute it. Muting the radio at work is a huge violation, though. You can miss a drop. Dropping things is the worst, especially the stretcher. You never, ever drop the stretcher.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, rapidly shifting topics from oxygen tanks to burning hair, tires, mud flaps, TV commercials, and stretchers.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies the grandiose delusion of being chosen or having a special understanding.

turns.doctor_question: When you are doing these sequences, do you ever wish you could stop doing them, even though you feel like you can't?
turns.patient_response: Stop doing them? I mean... I don't really think about stopping. It's just something you have to finish, you know? Like... like when you start an IV. Once you uncap the needle, you can't just stop halfway and put it down. You have to finish the stick, tape it down, flush the line. We use these new safety catheters now, they have this little button you push and the needle retracts into a plastic housing so you don't stick yourself. Needlestick injuries are a huge deal. You have to go through all this bloodwork, take prophylactic meds that make you feel like garbage. Garbage day in my neighborhood is Tuesday, but they always come super early, like 5:30 AM. The truck is so loud, it sounds like a jet engine right outside the window. Jets fly over my house all the time because we're on the flight path for the regional airport. Have you ever been to the airport, Doc? The security lines are ridiculous. They make you take off your shoes, which I hate because the floor is always freezing. Cold floors remind me of the hospital morgue. We have to take DOAs down there sometimes. It always smells like strong cleaner and... I don't know, just cold air. Air conditioning in the summer is great, though. Our rig's AC went out last August, and we were sweating through our uniforms by 9 AM.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe derailment and loose associations, shifting rapidly from IVs to garbage day, airplanes, the airport, the morgue, and air conditioning.

turns.doctor_question: When you are doing these sequences, does it ever make you feel frustrated, annoyed, or anxious that you are spending so much time on them instead of doing other things?
turns.patient_response: Frustrated? No, I don't really get frustrated. I just... I just have to do them. It's not about being annoyed, it's just the way it has to be done. Like washing the rig at the end of a shift. You have to scrub the tires, hose down the back. We use this heavy-duty soap, it comes in these big industrial drums. The drums are metal, and they make this loud hollow sound if you hit them. There was this kid in my neighborhood growing up who used to play the drums in his garage. He was terrible, just banging away for hours. His dad was a mechanic, had grease permanently stained into his hands. You know, no matter how much you scrub with that pumice soap, the grease just stays in the cracks of your skin. Skin is the largest organ in the human body, they teach you that on the first day of EMT school. Burns are the worst because the skin just sloughs right off. We had this call at a restaurant fire once... the grease trap caught. Grease fires are crazy, you can't put water on them or they just explode. Have you ever seen a grease fire explode, Doc? It's like a fireball. Fireballs remind me of those cinnamon candies, the little round ones. I hate cinnamon. It always makes my throat scratchy.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe derailment and loose associations, rapidly shifting topics from washing a rig to metal drums, a neighborhood kid, grease, skin, burns, a restaurant fire, and finally cinnamon candies.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient confirms engaging in compulsive 'sequences' that they feel driven to perform, stating 'I just have to do them' and 'it's just the way it has to be done'.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever get the feeling that the TV, the radio, or people around you are sending you special messages or signals that are meant just for you?
turns.patient_response: Special messages? No, I don't... I don't really get any messages like that. The TV is just the TV. I mean, the commercials are loud, like I said before, but they're just selling stuff. Car insurance, mostly. There's always a car insurance commercial on. Car accidents are the worst part of the job, honestly. Especially on the interstate when it's raining. People just don't know how to slow down when the roads are slick. Hydroplaning is terrifying. You just completely lose control of the steering wheel. Steering wheels are gross if you think about it. People eat in their cars, sneeze on their hands, and then just grab the wheel. We have to wipe down the steering wheel in the rig with these heavy-duty bleach wipes at the start of every shift. Bleach ruins your clothes if you're not careful. I got a drop of it on my favorite dark blue hoodie once, and it left this bright pink spot right on the front. Pink is such a weird color for bleach to turn things. Like, why pink? Flamingos are pink because of the shrimp they eat, did you know that? If they don't eat the shrimp, they just turn white. Shrimp is okay, but I can't stand cocktail sauce. Horseradish just burns your nose. Have you ever eaten too much horseradish at once? It feels like your sinuses are on fire.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting rapidly from TV commercials to car accidents, steering wheels, bleach, flamingos, and horseradish.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies receiving special messages from the TV or radio, stating 'The TV is just the TV'.
